name: Armada
lede: Armada is a very dark, warm brown, a textile color of the 1920s whose name recalls a fleet.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
The color is in Maerz and Paul's dictionary, first recorded in 1922, on plate 8 H 6; the neighbor Granada was recorded in 1924 on the same plate [1]. The name is Spanish for a fleet, and the best-known fleet is the Spanish Armada of 1588 [2][3].

No book we hold connects the color to that fleet [2][3]. Finlay mentions the Armada only in passing, noting that the English law banning logwood dyeing was passed in 1581 and the sea battle came in 1588 [3]. Greenfield places Philip II's Armada in the politics of the age of cochineal [2]. The color name's origin is undocumented. It is a close cousin of [[bistre]] and [[chestnut]] among dark browns [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Armada is one of the most common dark browns in our archive of 23,781 paintings, appearing in 15.05% of them, as photographed [4]. It is more common than 98% of the named colors, and peaks in the 1500s, in 15.6% of that century's paintings [4]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 39% of cases [4]. Its most devoted painter is Jacopo Bassano, in 7 of 14 works here [4]. Dark varnish deepens browns, so these numbers describe photographs of old canvases [4].

origin.named_after: origin undocumented; Spanish armada means fleet

notes.cite: ColorHub painting archive, 23,781 paintings, fieldnotes (as photographed)

questions.q: In which century does Armada peak in our painting archive?
The books we hold say the color Armada is named for the Spanish fleet of 1588.

openers: Armada appears in about one painting in seven in our archive, as photographed.
